name: n8n API Rate-Limit Manager - Dynamic Throttling

parameters.content:
## n8n API Rate-Limit Manager - Dynamic Throttling

A traffic governor for any external API your workflows call. Callers send requests to this webhook instead of the API directly. The manager enforces a per-service request budget in Redis and **adapts that budget automatically** from what the upstream API tells it (AIMD: additive increase, multiplicative decrease).

Over-budget requests are not simply dropped: if the next window opens soon enough they are **delayed** (throttled) and then released, otherwise they get a 429 with Retry-After.

### How the limit adapts
- Upstream returns **429** -> limit is cut (default x0.5, never below minLimit) and the service is put in **backoff** until Retry-After expires. Calls during backoff are rejected instantly.
- Upstream says **remaining / limit < 10%** (X-RateLimit-* headers) -> limit is trimmed by 20%.
- Healthy responses -> limit creeps back up by increaseStepPercent of baseLimit, at most once per window, until it reaches baseLimit again.

### How to set up
1. Import this workflow into n8n
2. Add the Redis credential on every Redis node
3. Edit Set - Limiter Config: serviceRegistry (service -> baseUrl, baseLimit, windowSeconds, minLimit, maxWaitSeconds, optional static headers) and the global defaults
4. Point callers at POST /webhook/rate-limit-manager with body { service, path, method, payload }
5. Activate the workflow

### Redis keys
- `rl:{service}:state` - JSON { limit, blockedUntil, lastAdjusted, lastReason }
- `rl:{service}:win:{bucket}` - request counter for the current window (TTL = 2 x window)

### How to customize
- Raise or lower maxWaitSeconds per service to trade latency for fewer 429s (keep it below your proxy / client timeout)
- Replace the fixed window with a token bucket if you need smoother bursts
- Add priority classes (e.g. reserve capacity for interactive requests)
- Use n8n credentials rather than registry headers for secrets
- Redis errors fail OPEN (requests are allowed) so a Redis outage never blocks your integrations

## 1. Trigger, Config & Service Registry

Webhook - Limiter Entry receives { service, path, method, payload }.

Set - Limiter Config holds global defaults and the serviceRegistry (the only hosts this workflow can call, so it cannot be abused as an open proxy).

JS - Resolve Service validates the service/path, merges per-service overrides with defaults and derives the Redis keys.

IF - Service Registered sends unknown services / bad paths to a 404.

## 2. Dynamic Limit & Backoff Check

Redis - Get Limiter State loads the adaptive state for the service.

JS - Compute Effective Limit works out the current limit (falls back to baseLimit) and whether an upstream backoff from an earlier 429 is still active.

IF - Upstream Backoff Active rejects calls instantly while the upstream is asking us to back off.

## 3. Quota Check

Redis - Increment Window Counter does an atomic INCR on the current window bucket.

JS - Evaluate Quota compares the count with the effective limit, works out seconds until the window resets, and decides whether the request can be delayed.

## 4. Throttle (Delay, then Release)

If the next window opens within maxWaitSeconds the request waits (with a little jitter), claims a slot in the new window and is released. If that slot is also over budget, or the wait would be too long, the caller gets a 429.

## 5. Call Upstream & Adapt Limit

HTTP Request - Call Upstream API never throws on HTTP errors so headers and status always reach the adapter.

JS - Adapt Limit applies AIMD using the status code and X-RateLimit-* / Retry-After headers. Only changed state is written back to Redis, so healthy steady-state traffic costs one INCR and one GET.

## 6. Response

Success returns the upstream result with rate-limit metadata and X-RateLimit-* / X-Throttle-Delay headers. An upstream 429 is passed on as a 429 with Retry-After.
